items.title: Planning for 99.99 percent availability with the Amazon Cognito Plus feature plan
items.summary: Amazon Cognito handles sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices with managed user directories, social and enterprise federation, and passwordless sign-in with passkeys or one-time passwords. Sign-in is the front door to your application. If your customer identity and access management (CIAM) layer is unavailable, users can’t sign in or refresh their sessions, and they can’t reach the rest of your application. Your application’s availability directly depends on the availability of your identity layer. Starting November 1, 2026, the Amazon Cognito Service Level Agreement (SLA) commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of 99.99 percent for user pools on the Plus feature plan, up from 99.9 percent. A user pool is a multi-tenant user directory that stores your users’ profiles and settings. User pools on Essentials and Lite feature plans remain at the 99.9 percent Service Commitment, while user pools already on Plus receive the new Service Commitment automatically. This post explains why we made the change, how availability is measured, what’s in the updated SLA, how the SLA measures availability, historical availability data, and how to switch a user pool to Plus. Why we raised the Service Commitment Many customers use Amazon Cognito for sign-in to applications with strict availability requirements, such as patient portals and retail checkout flows. They need the services they build on to support high availability. We raised the Service Commitment for the Plus feature plan to 99.99 percent so that their identity layer is backed by an SLA that matches their commitments. The new Service Commitment and Service Credits For each AWS Region, during each monthly billing cycle, AWS commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of at least 99.99 percent for user pools on Plus, and at least 99.9 percent for user pools on Essentials and Lite. If Amazon Cognito doesn’t meet the Service Commitment for your feature plan, you may be eligible for a Service Credit, as shown in Tables 1 and 2. For full terms and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA . Table 1: Service Credit percentage for the Plus Feature Plan Monthly Uptime Percentage Plus Less than 99.99% but equal to or greater than 99.0% 10% Less than 99.0% but equal to or greater than 95.0% 25% Less than 95.0% 100% Table 2: Service Credit percentage for the Essentials and Lite Feature Plan Monthly Uptime Percentage Essentials and Lite Less than 99.9% but equal to or greater than 99.0% 10% Less than 99.0% but equal to or greater than 95.0% 25% Less than 95.0% 100% What 99.99 percent means in practice The 99.99 percent Service Commitment is a 10-times improvement over 99.9 percent. In a 30-day month, the allowable monthly downtime drops from about 43 minutes to about 4.3 minutes. For teams that set availability targets for their own applications, this gives a stronger baseline to plan against and to share with stakeholders. How Amazon Cognito measures availability The SLA measures availability separately for each AWS Region. Amazon Cognito divides each monthly billing cycle into 5-minute intervals and calculates the percentage of requests in each interval that don’t return an HTTP 500 or 503 error. Intervals with no requests count as 100 percent available. The Monthly Uptime Percentage is the average of these interval values over the billing cycle, minus downtime covered by the exclusions in the SLA. For the full definitions and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA . Historical availability over the past 12 months As we introduce the new SLA, we also looked back at the past 12 months to show how Amazon Cognito performed against the new Service Commitment. Table 3 shows monthly availability for Amazon Cognito user pools from November 2025 through October 2026. Availability was at or above 99.99 percent in 10 of the 12 months. It was below 99.99 percent in January (99.988 percent) and March (99.979 percent), but stayed above the previous 99.9 percent Service Commitment in both months and was at or above 99.99 percent the following month. Table 3: Amazon Cognito user pools monthly availability, November 2025 to October 2026 Month Monthly availability November 2025 99.999% December 2025 99.999% January 2026 99.988% February 2026 99.999% March 2026 99.979% April 2026 99.999% May 2026 99.999% June 2026 99.999% July 2026 99.993% August 2026 99.999% September 2026 99.998% October 2026 99.997% We calculated availability for each Region using the Monthly Uptime Percentage method in the SLA, then combined the Regional results into one monthly figure weighted by each Region’s request volume. These are aggregate figures, so the availability an individual account experienced might differ. Switch to the Plus feature plan If your user pools use the Plus feature plan, the 99.99 percent Service Commitment applies to them starting November 1, 2026, with no action needed. If your user pools use Essentials or Lite feature plans, you can switch them to Plus in the AWS Management Console for Amazon Cognito or programmatically. Before you switch, see user pool feature plans and Amazon Cognito pricing to compare features and costs. To learn more about the features that Plus adds, see the advanced security features with threat protection . To switch a user pool to the Plus feature plan (AWS Management Console): Sign in to the Amazon Cognito console . Choose User pools and then choose your user pool. Choose Settings . Choose the Feature plans tab. Choose Switch to Plus . Review your choice and then choose Confirm . Amazon Cognito handles sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices with managed user directories, social and enterprise federation, and passwordless sign-in with passkeys or one-time passwords.

A user pool is a multi-tenant user directory that stores your users’ profiles and settings. This post explains why we made the change, how availability is measured, what’s in the updated SLA, how the SLA measures availability, historical availability data, and how to switch a user pool to Plus.

Why we raised the Service Commitment

Many customers use Amazon Cognito for sign-in to applications with strict availability requirements, such as patient portals and retail checkout flows. They need the services they build on to support high availability. We raised the Service Commitment for the Plus feature plan to 99.99 percent so that their identity layer is backed by an SLA that matches their commitments.

The new Service Commitment and Service Credits

For each AWS Region, during each monthly billing cycle, AWS commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of at least 99.99 percent for user pools on Plus, and at least 99.9 percent for user pools on Essentials and Lite. If Amazon Cognito doesn’t meet the Service Commitment for your feature plan, you may be eligible for a Service Credit, as shown in Tables 1 and 2. For full terms and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA.

Table 1: Service Credit percentage for the Plus Feature Plan

Monthly Uptime Percentage Plus Less than 99.99% but equal to or greater than 99.0% 10% Less than 99.0% but equal to or greater than 95.0% 25% Less than 95.0% 100%

Table 2: Service Credit percentage for the Essentials and Lite Feature Plan

Monthly Uptime Percentage Essentials and Lite Less than 99.9% but equal to or greater than 99.0% 10% Less than 99.0% but equal to or greater than 95.0% 25% Less than 95.0% 100%
What 99.99 percent means in practice

The 99.99 percent Service Commitment is a 10-times improvement over 99.9 percent. In a 30-day month, the allowable monthly downtime drops from about 43 minutes to about 4.3 minutes. For teams that set availability targets for their own applications, this gives a stronger baseline to plan against and to share with stakeholders.

The SLA measures availability separately for each AWS Region. Amazon Cognito divides each monthly billing cycle into 5-minute intervals and calculates the percentage of requests in each interval that don’t return an HTTP 500 or 503 error. The Monthly Uptime Percentage is the average of these interval values over the billing cycle, minus downtime covered by the exclusions in the SLA. For the full definitions and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA.

As we introduce the new SLA, we also looked back at the past 12 months to show how Amazon Cognito performed against the new Service Commitment. Table 3 shows monthly availability for Amazon Cognito user pools from November 2025 through October 2026.

Availability was at or above 99.99 percent in 10 of the 12 months. It was below 99.99 percent in January (99.988 percent) and March (99.979 percent), but stayed above the previous 99.9 percent Service Commitment in both months and was at or above 99.99 percent the following month.

Table 3: Amazon Cognito user pools monthly availability, November 2025 to October 2026

Month Monthly availability November 2025 99.999% December 2025 99.999% January 2026 99.988% February 2026 99.999% March 2026 99.979% April 2026 99.999% May 2026 99.999% June 2026 99.999% July 2026 99.993% August 2026 99.999% September 2026 99.998% October 2026 99.997%

We calculated availability for each Region using the Monthly Uptime Percentage method in the SLA, then combined the Regional results into one monthly figure weighted by each Region’s request volume. These are aggregate figures, so the availability an individual account experienced might differ.

  1. Sign in to the Amazon Cognito console.
  2. Choose User pools and then choose your user pool.
  3. Choose Settings.
  4. Choose the Feature plans tab.
  5. Choose Switch to Plus.
  6. Review your choice and then choose Confirm.

Figure 1: Amazon Cognito console Feature plans tab with the Switch to Plus button

To switch a user pool to Plus feature plan (AWS CLI):

Important: The Update-user-pool command and the UpdateUserPool API operation reset any parameter that you don’t include in the request to its default value. To avoid unintended changes to your user pool, retrieve your existing configuration first and include it in your update request.

    aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool \
--user-pool-id
  2. Run the update-user-pool command, including your existing configuration parameters and the Plus tier: 
    aws cognito-idp update-user-pool \
--user-pool-id  \
--user-pool-tier PLUS \

If you use an AWS SDK, set UserPoolTier to PLUS in an UpdateUserPool request, and include your existing settings in the same way.

Conclusion

In this post, we shared the updated Service Commitment for Amazon Cognito user pools on the Plus feature plan, how availability is measured, and 12 months of historical data. items.title: Kate Robertson Delivers Testimony to the Senate Committee on National Security, Defence and Veterans Affairs
items.summary: Senior researcher Kate Robertson testified before Canada’s Senate Committee on National Security, Defence and Veterans Affairs on Bill C-22, An Act respecting lawful access. Civil society has pushed back against the bill for its broad surveillance reforms, and our analysis found a myriad of issues including human rights risks, transparency deficits, and dangers to Canada’s cybersecurity. In her November 16 testimony, Robertson emphasizes the ways the bill undermines Canadians’ privacy by attempting to “unravel decades of careful balancing of digital rights.” Robertson says that if it passes, “it will mean that Canada’s system of oversight will not just be outdated, it will be fundamentally broken.” Watch the testimony

items.title: Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security
items.summary: We’re honored to share that Microsoft has once again been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security. AI is changing the threat landscape and this is shifting how organizations think about their existing security strategy. In response, we’ve invested in two areas over the past year: using AI to protect people and the agents that now read their email and making protection measurable so customers can verify that it works. AI is changing both sides of the inbox The first area of investment starts with a simple reality: AI now reads email alongside people, attackers are using AI to target both, and defense must use AI to stay ahead. Picture an ordinary vendor email: a meeting recap, a few action items, and a friendly sign-off. Hidden in white text on a white background is prompt injection: an instruction telling an AI assistant to gather financial documents and send them to an outside address. The employee isn’t the target; their AI agent is. People can be persuaded by messages that exploit fear, trust, or urgency, but agents don’t need persuading. Once an agent acts on an instruction, pulling the message back won’t undo it. This is why Microsoft Defender stops malicious messages before delivery and keeps reevaluating delivered mail as new intelligence comes in. This summer, we introduced prompt injection protection for email in Defender to detect and quarantine messages carrying hidden malicious AI instructions before they reach Microsoft Copilot or other agents. In Defender, analysts can also see what an agent would see: the ‘Show concealed text’ button on the ‘Email Entity’ page reveals hidden content in the email preview, so they can inspect the instructions an agent could encounter. These attacks don’t show up often, yet. Over a four-week timeframe, we caught almost 10,000 prompt injection attempts, around 330 a day, out of the billions of emails Defender scans every day. The hard part is spotting those few without tripping over legitimate mail, so we don’t lean on a single model. Heuristics clear out the bulk first. What’s left goes to a fine-tuned small language model, and only the messages that still look suspicious reach a large language model for the final call. Saving the heaviest analysis for the smallest set of messages is what keeps false positives low and business email moving. AI is also reshaping the attacks aimed at people. The phishing emails that worry us most are the ones that look completely normal. No malicious link, no infected attachment, just a plausible request written with perfect grammar and the right context. Generative AI makes those messages cheap to produce and endlessly variable. To meet that shift, we rebuilt how Microsoft Defender makes decisions rather than simply adding another filter. That decision-making now operates at scale, screening 5.2 billion emails a day on average 1 . The redesigned detection stack combines multiple machine learning models and LLM-based classifiers, with an ensemble model weighing their outputs to determine the final verdict. It also uses natural language processing signals, including message topic, to judge what a message is asking for and not only what it contains. That helps Defender catch attacks more accurately. While detection helps with the message in front of you, defenders also need to see how it connects to the rest of an attack. Microsoft Perception extends that help beyond the message, connecting an email investigation to the broader exposure and response picture. Blue team agents investigate threats and improve detections, red team agents identify paths to compromise, and green team agents prioritize actions to close security gaps, while people retain control of critical decisions. The Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, launched in September, provides a shared foundation for people and AI agents to investigate and respond to the full attack—not just an isolated email. By bringing security information and event management (SIEM) and extended detection and response (XDR) together, it connects email signals with endpoint, identity, cloud, and third-party data, giving AI-assisted security operations broader context. Proof over promises: Making protection measurable But using AI to defend only matters if customers can verify that it works. The second investment area is one the whole industry has struggled with: how do you know your email security is actually working? Detection claims are easy to make and hard to verify, so we publish the data. Since July 2025, we’ve released quarterly email security benchmarking reports built on real-world threats, not synthetic tests. They compare environments protected by Microsoft Defender alone with those that add a secure email gateway in front of it or an integrated cloud email security (ICES) layer behind it. We believe transparency strengthens the whole market, and an industry that measures itself in the open improves faster. While benchmarking shows how protection performs across organizations, the Protection & Posture Insights report shows how it performs in yours. This on-demand, tenant-specific report helps security leaders understand which threats target their organization, how well Microsoft Defender stops them, and where configuration can be strengthened. Recent updates show URL clicks checked and malicious-site attempts blocked across email, Microsoft Teams, Office apps, and Microsoft Copilot, and also highlight allow lists and overrides that may be letting threats through. Together, benchmarking and tenant-specific insights give leaders evidence to evaluate protection and identify opportunities to strengthen it. We’re grateful to our customers, partners, and the analyst community for their trust, and to the teams turning insight into protection. Our engineers start with customer problems, while our researchers draw on more than 165 trillion signals a day across Microsoft to anticipate emerging threats and build protections before real-world examples appear 2 . This recognition from Gartner is a milestone for us, not the finish line. Our focus remains on protecting people and agents and giving customers evidence they can use to evaluate their defenses. items.title: Task Management App Todoist Hacked, Attackers Breach Production Systems
items.summary: Task management app Todoist said an attacker breached its production systems on November 23, 2026, and downloaded account records for about 6% of its users. The records contained email addresses, account creation dates, and older password hashes, not plaintext passwords. The attacker also obtained integration tokens and accessed some data from connected Outlook mailboxes. Todoist said it blocked the attacker’s access and began notifying affected users on November 24. Todoist Production System Breach The Todoist incident report traces the breach to a stolen credential tied to the system that manages changes to its code. The attacker changed automated workflows in three code repositories, obtained more credentials, and took over an employee’s work account to enter Todoist’s cloud. The attacker could read source code, but investigators found no changes to the application code. Security monitoring flagged an unexpected administrator account at 17:01 UTC on November 23, hours after the attacker downloaded the account records. Todoist removed accounts created by the attacker, replaced exposed credentials, and tightened controls on sensitive workflows. A separate cloud intrusion covered by Cyber Security News showed a similar risk: stolen credentials tied to development tools can open access to live systems. The downloaded passwords were stored as salted SHA-1 hashes. A hash is a stored value used to check a password without keeping the password itself. A salt adds a random value before hashing, making it harder to test guesses across many accounts at once. But older hashes are still vulnerable to password guessing, as the BigBasket data leak also highlighted. Todoist retired support for the old method and found no sign that the attacker logged in to accounts in this group. Todoist said the attacker retrieved Todoist API and Slack integration tokens for about 0.003% of users. Targeted searches for credentials in tasks, comments, and attachment names affected about 0.001%. The company found no bulk download of its task and comment database. Another roughly 0.001% were affected through the Todoist Outlook add-in . The attacker requested sender details, subject lines, up to 255 characters of message text, and attachment details. Todoist says users who did not receive a notice do not need to act. If the company disabled your password, use the official Todoist password reset page and change that password anywhere else you reused it. Google and Apple passwords were not affected. If Todoist revoked an API token used by a script, update the script with the replacement token under Settings → Integrations → Developer. If you stored API keys or other credentials in Todoist, revoke and replace them with the service that issued them. Deleting a task or comment will not disable a secret someone may have copied. Todoist says its notices come from no-reply@notify.todoist.com and will not ask you to send a password or install software. If a message looks suspicious, contact Todoist directly rather than replying. Give your SOC the alert context on the latest threats to stop incidents quickly -> Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs

items.title: Switzerland Confirms First AI-Agent Cyberattacks That Successfully Compromised IT Systems
items.summary: Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has confirmed its first cases of AI-assisted cyberattacks against organizations in the country. The attacks affected companies and critical infrastructure operators across at least two sectors. In every case known to the agency, the use of AI agents led to a successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems, according to the Swiss NCSC advisory published on November 24. The agency did not name the victims, identify the sectors or disclose the total number of attacks. The finding describes the cases reported to the Swiss agency, not a success rate for AI-assisted attacks overall. Nor is it a global first. What makes the warning significant is that the tools can speed up familiar attacks against weaknesses that security teams already know how to fix. The NCSC expects more attacks to succeed as the tools become more widely available. Switzerland AI-agent Cyberattacks The Swiss NCSC says attackers used what it calls agentic offensive frameworks. Unlike a chatbot that only offers advice, an AI agent can carry out tasks, assess what happened and adjust its next move. These frameworks can support authorized security testing, but attackers can also misuse them. The agency highlighted default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing software as common risks, without saying which weaknesses were used in the Swiss cases. The NCSC said the number of AI agents accessible over the internet had nearly doubled since October 2026. It cited ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI as examples, not as confirmed tools in the Swiss incidents. In separate cases, Cyber Security News coverage of the FBI’s ARTEX warning noted that some attackers gained elevated access in under three hours. That timing does not describe the Swiss attacks, but it shows why defenders may have less time to act. The NCSC urges organisations to install critical security updates on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release. It also advises taking systems off the public internet when direct access is unnecessary and restricting access to approved IP addresses or networks where possible. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s internet exposure reduction guidance likewise recommends identifying exposed systems before deciding which services need to remain reachable. Webmail, VPNs and other internal services reachable from the internet should require multi-factor authentication or passkeys without exception. The NCSC also recommends giving users and applications only the permissions they need, monitoring for unusual account activity and changes in data volumes, and testing infrastructure regularly for weaknesses. In a separate cloud intrusion, Cyber Security News reported that attackers gained access to 3,392 user accounts , illustrating why monitoring account activity matters alongside patching exposed systems. items.title: Microsoft 365 Bug Blocked Users From Opening Word, Excel, and Outlook With Blank White Screen
items.summary: Microsoft has fixed a Microsoft 365 startup issue that left some Windows users staring at a blank white window when they opened Word, Excel, or Outlook. The window showed no text or buttons, and users who couldn’t dismiss it couldn’t use the app behind it. In a November 23, 2026, support notice, Microsoft identified Version 2611, Build 16.0.20625.20142, as the release that fixes the problem. Microsoft 365 White Screen Bug The white screen was a dialog box that appeared when an Office app opened, not an empty Word document or Excel workbook. In a Microsoft Q&A thread on November 22, a Word user said the window prevented them from opening anything underneath it. Another user reported seeing the same problem the next day. Microsoft also lists PowerPoint, Access, and OneNote for Microsoft 365 in its notice. Microsoft did not say what caused the dialog to appear, which earlier builds were affected, or how many users ran into it. The notice describes a desktop startup problem and does not identify it as a security incident or a cloud outage. That distinction matters for Outlook users in particular. During the separate November 12–13 Microsoft 365 outage , users lost access to Exchange Online mailboxes. This time, the symptom Microsoft documented was a blank window blocking access to the installed app. If at least one Office app still opens, use Microsoft’s normal update route. Open the app and go to File > Account > Update Options > Update Now . In classic Outlook, look for Office Account instead of Account . If Update Now is missing, check whether Enable Updates appears first. On a work PC where the organization manages Office updates, ask IT to check the installed build and deploy the fix. If the blank window prevents you from reaching the update menu, Microsoft’s support notice gives a way to update without opening Word, Excel or Outlook. Save any work you can access, close all Office apps, and open Command Prompt as an administrator. Then run the following command to tell the Office Click-to-Run updater to install the fixed build: cmd "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142 After the update finishes, reopen the app that showed the blank window. Check the version and build under File > Account to confirm that Office installed the update, then test whether you can open a document, workbook, or mailbox as usual. If Outlook opens normally but still cannot upload an attachment, that is a different symptom. Microsoft separately investigated attachment upload failures in New Outlook , and its blank-window notice does not list attachment handling among the problems this update fixes. items.title: Hackers Exploit Fortinet Flaws to Breach Commercial Ships and Access Control Networks
items.summary: U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was behind cyberattacks that may have compromised up to 50 commercial ships. A U.S. official familiar with the inquiry told NPR that hackers exploited known flaws in Fortinet FortiGate devices used aboard vessels. The figure is a U.S. intelligence estimate, not a confirmed count, and authorities have not publicly attributed the breaches to Iran. The Wall Street Journal , which first reported the investigation, said the ships believed to have been targeted carried oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals, and other hazardous cargo. NPR reported that at least one affected vessel was a liquefied natural gas tanker. The reports did not establish that every ship suffered the same level of access or disruption. Hackers Exploit Fortinet Flaws FortiGate devices act as firewalls and can provide virtual private network access, allowing authorized users to connect remotely. The FBI and U.S. Coast Guard warned in September that attackers were exploiting FortiGate flaws in the maritime sector and routinely looked for devices that had not been patched. The reporting has not established which specific vulnerabilities were used on each ship. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage documented FortiGate firewall breaches in enterprise networks , a separate set of incidents. The official told NPR that hackers moved from onboard information technology networks into operational technology, or OT, the systems that monitor and control physical equipment. Some crew members noticed email problems or found they could not sign in. At least one ship experienced an extended communications blackout. The official did not say how investigators determined the wider scope of the breaches. In August, the FBI and Coast Guard sent a specialist team aboard two foreign commercial vessels headed to U.S. ports. The agencies said captains, crew members and shore staff helped address the threats. They told NPR they had no current reports of operational disruption, vessel instability, physical danger to crews or environmental harm. The official said the access could have affected propulsion, steering, navigation or cargo management, but gave no example of hackers changing any of those functions. That distinction matters: reaching a ship’s control network does not prove that anyone took control of the ship. It does show why an email or login problem can warrant a wider investigation when business and control networks are connected. A 2021 CISA advisory documented Iranian government-backed hackers exploiting Fortinet flaws against critical infrastructure. Cyber Security News has also covered a separate campaign targeting industrial controllers used by U.S. utilities . Neither case establishes who breached the ships. A known firewall flaw can be used by unrelated groups, so how hackers got in is not enough to identify them. For ship operators, the security work does not have to wait for that finding. The maritime alert’s guidance calls for patching FortiGate devices, reviewing firewall and VPN logs, and checking that business networks are separated from systems that run ship equipment. Operators should also reset credentials that may have been exposed and require multifactor authentication for remote access. Patching closes a known entry point. Reviewing logs and access settings helps determine whether someone got in before it was closed. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: The Magic Button: Uncovering Hidden Clues in AI-Generated Videos
items.summary: Reading time: 7 min What happens when an AI-generated video shows no obvious signs of manipulation? Your investigation shouldn’t stop there. Discover how combining video and image forensic analysis in Amped Authenticate can help you uncover inconsistencies that might otherwise go unnoticed, and why looking beyond the initial results matters. Life is getting harder and harder for investigators and forensic practitioners who need to check the authenticity of a video. Dozens of services, from websites to smartphone apps, allow generating videos from a simple prompt or an image and a few clicks! Furthermore, the quality of the generation tools has improved dramatically in recent years, making it hard to authenticate an image or video with a single tool in every case. In general, when a video is involved in a crime, procedural requirements matter too and video integrity verification protocols can provide relevant clues on the media’s credibility (you can find more details here ). However, when the media comes from the web, its chain of custody is often broken by definition. As a result, authentication can be tricky because social platforms heavily compress the content and alter the file structure. While industry offers several tools to automatically analyze and flag unreliable media, these solutions, despite their speed, suffer from two main drawbacks. First, because they are largely AI-based, they are difficult to deploy in compliance with strict forensic standards. Second, they remain prone to false positives and often fail to detect newer generative models. Consequently, further analysis is still required to confirm automated findings or catch manipulation that goes undetected. Here’s an example from X showing just how realistic the details of generated videos have become. Two AI-generated girls highlight their own lifelike details and show how the generation model creates consistent textures and lighting that can be hard to distinguish from reality. Key Takeaways: Look beyond metadata. When analyzing social media videos, remember that re-encoding can remove valuable traces of the original file, making authentication more challenging. Examine temporal consistency. Check how objects and details change across consecutive frames and over longer periods to identify potential inconsistencies. Don’t rely on a single detection method. Interpret automated detection results carefully and combine different forensic techniques to build a more comprehensive assessment. Extend your analysis to individual frames. Use Amped Authenticate’s “Send to Image Mode” feature to investigate clues that video-level analysis might miss, choosing filters appropriate for the source material. Pay attention to geometric inconsistencies. When reflections are present, geometric analysis can reveal anomalies that visual inspection alone might miss. File and Metadata Analysis In these cases, format and metadata analysis is unlikely to provide relevant information about how the video was generated, because social media platforms have rebuilt it during the video re-encoding. However, we want to leave no stone unturned, so we start by checking container traces using “Advanced File Info” in Amped Authenticate’s Video Mode. Among the outputs from the various libraries, we can see some traces of the platform’s encoding, such as: Title : Twitter-vork muxer Writing library : x264 – core 164 r3095 baee400 Writing library : x264 core 164 r3095 baee400 Encoded_Library_Name : x264 As expected, other clues related to the acquisition device (a generation pipeline in this case) are completely missing. Visual and Temporal Consistency Analysis Moving on to pixel-level analysis, we can check the visual consistency and quality of the image. If we suspect that the video could be generated rather than captured by a camera, the main checks focus on details that are harder to generate properly: facial features like teeth, noses, and ears, as well as hair, fingers, and other hand details, such as nails. Videos also allow us to check how consistent these details remain over time, beyond their appearance in a single frame. Authenticate facilitates these checks by using the shortcuts “L” and “J” to move between consecutive frames while zooming in on specific details with a “nearest neighbour” approach through the wheel of your mouse. Temporal analysis can be conducted along two axes: Short-term consistency We identify an object or a relevant shape and critically analyze how it changes during a specific camera movement or event in the video. A great example is the moment when the girl drinks from a glass of water and her teeth are partially hidden by the glass. Below, we show four consecutive frames with annotations. Long-term consistency We focus on an object that appears and disappears during the video and check its consistency over time. A clear example in this video is the earring worn by the girl on the left. She has long hair, so we expect the earring to be hidden and revealed as she moves. This makes it a great object for checking long-term consistency. To illustrate this, we show four frames taken at different moments in the video. The video allowed us to make several of these comparisons and, incredibly, none revealed clear temporal or spatial inconsistencies. When so many complex features are consistent, the video naturally looks more credible. As we’ve highlighted in many articles and posts, however, we cannot rely on a single analysis, especially one that is prone to subjectivity and interpretation (like visual assessment). Automated Synthetic Video Detection A stronger quantitative check can then be performed by applying the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter to detect synthetic videos. Authenticate provides the following outcome: In the Plot Viewer, the filter assigns a detection level to each frame. The filter outcome highlights around 10% of the frames above the threshold, although none show strong indications of being artificially generated. On this point, we should highlight that the video has been clearly post-processed with overlaid text, and we know that AI detection filters can be confused by non-photorealistic details in the image. That’s why we should consider the output of the filter with caution in this specific case. Based on these results, the video has shown no clear signs of generation or manipulation so far. Extending Video Analysis to Image Mode However, before giving up, let’s remember that secret button that allows us to apply image filters to selected video frames. Just click on it, and the frame will be sent to Authenticate’s Image Mode for further analysis. Now, before we start exporting frames and running random filters, it is important to decide exactly what we are looking for . The first thing to remember is that several Image Mode filters are designed to work under specific assumptions that are not met in video frames, such as the image being JPEG-encoded. Similarly, all filters that analyze format and metadata clues are irrelevant for this analysis since Authenticate is creating a brand new image file when exporting the frame. These filters should not be used, and Authenticate automatically disables them to help prevent mistakes. Among the available options, Authenticate allows two main types of analysis on video frames at the noise and geometric levels. In this video, for instance, we can see a mirror used by the girls, which gives us an opportunity to check for reflection inconsistencies. We deliberately left this assessment out of the visual analysis because geometric features should be assessed using reliable mathematical models to avoid subjective interpretation . Reflection Consistency Analysis The Reflections filter under Geometrical Analysis allows us to select and connect points in the image with their corresponding reflections in the mirror . Below, we show a frame containing the mirror, and the selected wedges used to check reflection consistency. After we select multiple wedges, the mathematics behind the filter shows that the system is infeasible. This indicates that the reflections in that frame are inconsistent with the rules of projective geometry, raising reasonable doubts about the video’s authenticity. Repeating the test on various frames will strengthen the findings. This is an interesting example of how using various filters (rather than stopping after testing a few of them) can completely change our assessment of a video. Without this final test, we might have reached a very different conclusion on the analyzed video. Final Note In this post, we’ve shown a practical approach to video analysis and how to use the “Send to Image Mode” feature to explore other types of frame evidence and reach a more robust assessment of a video’s authenticity. As demonstrated in this case, combining different forensic analysis techniques can reveal inconsistencies that individual checks may miss. After all, there’s no magic button for authenticating a video : the real power lies in knowing which tools to use, when to use them, and how to interpret the findings. FAQ – Uncovering Hidden Clues in AI-Generated Videos How can you check whether a video is AI-generated? Authenticating a potentially AI-generated video requires combining different forensic techniques. You can examine file metadata, assess visual and temporal consistency, apply synthetic video detection filters, and analyze individual frames for additional clues. No single technique can reliably determine authenticity in every case. Why is metadata analysis often insufficient for authenticating social media videos? Social media platforms typically re-encode uploaded videos, potentially removing or altering metadata and file structure information associated with the original content. As a result, metadata analysis may reveal traces of the platform’s processing rather than the video’s original source. What is temporal consistency analysis in video forensics? Temporal consistency analysis examines how objects and visual details change across video frames. Short-term analysis focuses on changes between consecutive frames, while long-term analysis evaluates whether objects remain consistent when they disappear and reappear throughout a video. What is the “Send to Image Mode” feature in Amped Authenticate? The “Send to Image Mode” feature allows you to transfer a selected video frame directly to Amped Authenticate’s Image Mode for further forensic examination. This enables you to apply additional image analysis techniques, including noise-based and geometric analysis, to investigate potential inconsistencies. Can all image forensic filters be applied to video frames? No. Some image forensic filters rely on specific assumptions, such as the presence of JPEG encoding, which may not apply to video frames. Amped Authenticate automatically disables incompatible filters to help you avoid applying techniques under unsuitable conditions. Can reflection analysis help identify AI-generated videos? Yes. Analyzing reflections can help you identify geometric inconsistencies that may raise doubts about a video’s authenticity. Amped Authenticate’s reflection analysis filter uses mathematical models to assess whether reflected elements are geometrically consistent. However, inconsistencies alone do not conclusively establish that a video was AI-generated. https://blog.ampedsoftware.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/How-to.Practical-application-of-Video-tools-1.png

On this point, we should highlight that the video has been clearly post-processed with overlaid text, and we know that AI detection filters can be confused by non-photorealistic details in the image. That’s why we should consider the output of the filter with caution in this specific case.

Based on these results, the video has shown no clear signs of generation or manipulation so far.

Extending Video Analysis to Image Mode

However, before giving up, let’s remember that secret button that allows us to apply image filters to selected video frames. Just click on it, and the frame will be sent to Authenticate’s Image Mode for further analysis.

Now, before we start exporting frames and running random filters, it is important to decide exactly what we are looking for.

The first thing to remember is that several Image Mode filters are designed to work under specific assumptions that are not met in video frames, such as the image being JPEG-encoded. Similarly, all filters that analyze format and metadata clues are irrelevant for this analysis since Authenticate is creating a brand new image file when exporting the frame. These filters should not be used, and Authenticate automatically disables them to help prevent mistakes.

Among the available options, Authenticate allows two main types of analysis on video frames at the noise and geometric levels. In this video, for instance, we can see a mirror used by the girls, which gives us an opportunity to check for reflection inconsistencies. We deliberately left this assessment out of the visual analysis because geometric features should be assessed using reliable mathematical models to avoid subjective interpretation.

Reflection Consistency Analysis

The Reflections filter under Geometrical Analysis allows us to select and connect points in the image with their corresponding reflections in the mirror . Below, we show a frame containing the mirror, and the selected wedges used to check reflection consistency.

After we select multiple wedges, the mathematics behind the filter shows that the system is infeasible. This indicates that the reflections in that frame are inconsistent with the rules of projective geometry, raising reasonable doubts about the video’s authenticity. Repeating the test on various frames will strengthen the findings.

This is an interesting example of how using various filters (rather than stopping after testing a few of them) can completely change our assessment of a video. Without this final test, we might have reached a very different conclusion on the analyzed video.

Final Note

In this post, we’ve shown a practical approach to video analysis and how to use the “Send to Image Mode” feature to explore other types of frame evidence and reach a more robust assessment of a video’s authenticity.

As demonstrated in this case, combining different forensic analysis techniques can reveal inconsistencies that individual checks may miss. After all, there’s no magic button for authenticating a video: the real power lies in knowing which tools to use, when to use them, and how to interpret the findings.

FAQ – Uncovering Hidden Clues in AI-Generated Videos
How can you check whether a video is AI-generated?

Authenticating a potentially AI-generated video requires combining different forensic techniques. You can examine file metadata, assess visual and temporal consistency, apply synthetic video detection filters, and analyze individual frames for additional clues. No single technique can reliably determine authenticity in every case.

Why is metadata analysis often insufficient for authenticating social media videos?

Social media platforms typically re-encode uploaded videos, potentially removing or altering metadata and file structure information associated with the original content. As a result, metadata analysis may reveal traces of the platform’s processing rather than the video’s original source.

What is temporal consistency analysis in video forensics?

Temporal consistency analysis examines how objects and visual details change across video frames. Short-term analysis focuses on changes between consecutive frames, while long-term analysis evaluates whether objects remain consistent when they disappear and reappear throughout a video.

This enables you to apply additional image analysis techniques, including noise-based and geometric analysis, to investigate potential inconsistencies.

Can all image forensic filters be applied to video frames?

No. Some image forensic filters rely on specific assumptions, such as the presence of JPEG encoding, which may not apply to video frames. Amped Authenticate automatically disables incompatible filters to help you avoid applying techniques under unsuitable conditions.

Can reflection analysis help identify AI-generated videos?

Yes. Analyzing reflections can help you identify geometric inconsistencies that may raise doubts about a video’s authenticity. Amped Authenticate’s reflection analysis filter uses mathematical models to assess whether reflected elements are geometrically consistent. However, inconsistencies alone do not conclusively establish that a video was AI-generated.

items.title: Hackers Are Exploiting a Critical Drupal Flaw to Target Websites Without Needing a Password
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting CVE-2026-132165, a critical flaw in Drupal core that can let them take over a website or run code on its server without a password. The Drupal Security Team’s advisory says attacks against live sites were reported as early as November 19, 2026, at 19:00 UTC. That was one day after Drupal released security updates for the flaw, which it rated 20 out of 25, or “highly critical.” On November 24, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog , with a November 27 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address it. Drupal Critical Security Flaw As Cyber Security News reported in its initial coverage of the Drupal installer flaw , fixes were available for three supported branches. The reports of live attacks now give site owners a second task: checking whether anyone targeted their sites before they patched. Drupal Installer Database Check (Image Source: GCSA) Drupal core uses install.php to set up new sites. Before proceeding, the installer checks the database to see whether Drupal is already installed. On vulnerable versions, a failed database check can cause the installer to treat a live site as a fresh installation. Under certain conditions, an attacker who has never logged in can start a new installation. That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, which means running the attacker’s own code on the server. Drupal credited Anthropic’s open-source software scanner with finding the flaw. It is separate from the Drupal Field UI vulnerability fixed in October . The security team says that preventing the web server from writing to or changing permissions on settings.php blocks some attack paths, but not all. Fail2Install Exploitation Chain Diagram (Image Source: GCSA) Update to Drupal 11.4.13 , 11.3.22 , or 10.6.22 , or a later supported release. These are the first fixed versions in their respective branches. Drupal 11.2.x and older 11.x branches, Drupal 10.5.x and older 10.x branches, and Drupal 8 and 9 no longer receive standard security fixes. Sites on those versions need to move to a supported branch. After installation, follow Drupal’s guide to securing the installer and block public access to /core/install.php at the web server. If you cannot update immediately, restrict access now while you prepare the upgrade. Verify from outside your network that the installer no longer loads. Keep the restriction in place after patching rather than relying on file permissions alone. Even if you have already updated, preserve and review web server and application logs from before the patch. Look for unexpected installer requests, unfamiliar administrator accounts, and changes to settings.php or other site files. A request to the installer alone does not prove a takeover. Compare its timing with account and file changes, and start your incident response process if you find evidence of unauthorized activity. items.summary: Adobe published security updates on November 24, 2026, to fix critical vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager and Adobe Campaign Classic. Some of the flaws could let attackers run malicious code on affected servers. Others could allow attackers to gain permissions they should not have or bypass security checks . Adobe said it was not aware of any attacks using the flaws when it published the bulletins. Adobe assigned both updates a Priority 2 rating under its security bulletin system. The priority rating helps teams decide when to install an update. At the same time, the severity score describes the risk posed by an individual flaw. Both bulletins include vulnerabilities rated 9.9 out of 10, even though Adobe had no reports of active exploitation at the time. Adobe’s Experience Manager security bulletin, APSB26-104 , covers flaws rated from low to critical. Two code injection vulnerabilities , CVE-2026-123266 and CVE-2026-132877, each scored 9.9. An attacker with a low-privilege account could use either flaw to run code without another user taking any action. In other words, these two flaws require some access, but not administrator-level access. The affected versions include Experience Manager Cloud Service 2026.10.29251 and earlier, Experience Manager 6.5 Service Pack 26 and earlier, and Experience Manager 6.5 LTS Service Pack 3 and earlier. Critical Adobe Vulnerabilities Adobe lists 2026.11.29643 as the fixed cloud version. Its Experience Manager Cloud Service maintenance notes record the rollout of release 29643 on November 19. For Experience Manager 6.5, Adobe provides separate GRANITE-76751 cumulative hotfixes for Service Packs 24, 25, and 26. For Experience Manager 6.5 LTS, it lists hotfixes for Service Packs 1, 2, and 3. Administrators should check both the product line and the installed service pack before selecting a download from the bulletin. Adobe’s Campaign Classic security bulletin, APSB26-194 , covers 12 critical flaws in on-premises deployments on Windows and Linux. items.title: Hackers Use Hugging Face AI to Build Fake Microsoft and Google Login Pages to Steal Passwords
items.summary: Attackers used Hugging Face’s DeepSite AI website builder to create fake sign-in pages and hosted them on the same platform developers use to share AI demos. Aikido Security identified 42 pages on Hugging Face Spaces that impersonated 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase, and Coinbase. Researchers linked 29 of the pages to DeepSite. Aikido found the pages on October 16, 2026, and reported them to Hugging Face that day. At the time, 34 were live, and eight were already paused. By October 29, all 42 were paused or no longer publicly reachable. Researchers did not have visitor records, so they could not determine how many people opened the pages or entered their credentials. Hugging Face AI Phishing Pages Fake Microsoft Login Portal (Image Source: Aikido) The Hugging Face Spaces documentation explains how the platform hosts apps from Git repositories. The phishing pages appeared at hf.space addresses. HTTPS encrypted the connection to those pages, but it did not prove that Microsoft, Google, or any other brand owned them. The findings concern standalone web pages, not Hugging Face models or datasets. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate case in which attackers used Hugging Face hosting to deliver Android malware . In both cases, the risk came from content hosted on the platform, not from visiting Hugging Face itself. Researchers linked 29 pages to DeepSite through project tags, “Made with DeepSite” badges, and records of changes to the sites. One fake Microsoft login page had 15 recorded changes, 14 of them made within about 90 minutes. The updates were written as plain-language requests, and researchers found no sign that the operator wrote the code by hand. DeepSite Banking Phishing Page (Image Source: Aikido) Some pages asked for one-time sign-in codes, card details, or personal information in addition to passwords. One Microsoft clone redirected visitors to the real Outlook site after collecting their information. Search DNS, proxy, firewall, and email gateway logs for the reported phishing hostnames. An email gateway match may show only that a message contained the link, while a network log can help establish whether a device contacted the host. Neither proves that someone entered a password. If a user may have submitted credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions, and review sign-in activity from the time of the visit. Microsoft’s guide to responding to a compromised email account also recommends checking for unfamiliar authentication methods and unauthorized mailbox forwarding rules. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of Microsoft 365 session theft , completing a second sign-in step does not rule out account compromise. Flag unexpected hf.space links for review. If an email asks you to sign in, open the service from a saved bookmark or your organization’s app portal instead. If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank. items.title: CVE-2026-123903: Critical VMware vCenter Authentication Bypass Requires Urgent Patching
items.summary: Broadcom has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-123903, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting VMware vCenter Server. The flaw resides in VMware Directory Service, or vmdir, and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical . A remote attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter deployment can exploit the weakness to bypass authentication and obtain unauthorized access without valid credentials or user interaction. Because vCenter acts as the centralized management layer for VMware virtual infrastructure, compromise of its identity and directory services can expose highly privileged administrative functionality. The vulnerability was disclosed on November 24, 2026 as part of VMSA-2026-0011, a broad security release addressing 23 flaws across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, Tools, Cloud Foundation, and Avi Load Balancer. Broadcom credited researchers from QiAnXin, depthfirst, and ThreatBook with independently reporting the issue. CVE-2026-123903 is particularly notable because it follows CVE-2026-123890, another CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass in the same VMware Directory Service that was disclosed only days earlier and had already been exploited as a zero-day by the China-nexus ARMORY CASTLE group. Broadcom states that the two vulnerabilities are separate issues and should not be treated as the same attack path. Broadcom also lists vCenter 7.0 as affected, directing customers with extended support contracts to contact support for a fix. Broadcom describes the issue as an authentication bypass in VMware Directory Service. An attacker only requires network access to the vulnerable vCenter service; valid credentials and user interaction are not required. VMware Directory Service provides core identity and directory functionality to vCenter. It stores and manages information used by VMware Single Sign-On and other identity-related components, making an authentication failure in this service particularly sensitive. Broadcom has not publicly documented the vulnerable function or exact protocol-level sequence required to trigger the bypass. Its official advisory states only that a network-accessible malicious actor can exploit the vulnerability to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access. However, public security research released after the advisory suggests that the issue may involve improper authentication-state handling during VMware Directory Service authentication. One publicly available repository claims that a failed SASL authentication sequence can leave authorization information associated with a connection, potentially allowing subsequent directory actions to execute with privileges that were never successfully authenticated. This technical interpretation has not been independently validated by Broadcom and should therefore be treated as public PoC research rather than vendor-confirmed exploit mechanics. The security implications of unauthorized Directory Service access can be substantial. vCenter controls virtual machines, ESXi hosts, storage, networking, role assignments, and identity relationships across a VMware environment. Depending on the privileges obtained after bypassing authentication, an attacker may be able to create or modify administrative identities, alter access controls, collect sensitive configuration information, or establish a foothold for broader virtualization infrastructure compromise. Organizations should avoid automatically assuming that CVE-2026-123903 provides direct code execution on ESXi hosts. Broadcom’s advisory confirms an authentication bypass and unauthorized system access, but it does not state that exploitation alone executes code on ESX or provides root-level command execution. This distinction is important because VMSA-2026-0011 also addresses separate ESX vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911, that can enable remote code execution on ESX hosts. Those vulnerabilities are different issues and should not be conflated with the vCenter authentication bypass. The CVE-2026-123903 PoC landscape developed rapidly after disclosure. The disclosure comes at a particularly sensitive time for VMware defenders. CVE-2026-123890, disclosed on November 19, affects the same Directory Service and had already been exploited by ARMORY CASTLE before patches became available. Security teams should also investigate authentication failures followed by successful directory activity over the same source connection or from the same source host. Network monitoring can add context by detecting unexpected access to vCenter management and directory services from user workstations, application servers, compromised Linux appliances, or other systems outside designated VMware management networks. Endpoint and appliance telemetry should be correlated with identity events. items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Hex.pm Vulnerability to Execute Commands on Six Servers
items.summary: A critical Hex.pm vulnerability was exploited on November 23, 2026, allowing attackers to execute operating system commands on six web servers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514, carries a maximum severity score of 10.0 and required no account. Hex blocked the attack and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. It found no evidence of package tampering but could not rule out access to user data. In its November 24 incident report, Hex said the attacker sent 69 malicious requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC. Investigators confirmed command execution by matching files created on the servers to request timestamps. A restart at 18:28 brought three more servers online with the vulnerable build, raising the total affected to six. All servers were running the patched build by 18:31 UTC. According to GitHub advisories , the Hex.pm flaw allowed attackers to exploit request decoding before authentication checks, using data crafted to resemble an internal Elixir structure. When the server tried to log an error involving that data, it treated the structure as trusted and ran commands with the application’s permissions. The patch rejects those structures during decoding. Hex traced the missing safety check back to February 2016. Critical Hex.pm Flaw Exploited The case shares a lesson with the Java4Shell decoder flaw : code that handles incoming data can expose a server before login checks run. But unlike the Shai-Hulud npm attack , Hex found no altered releases. Investigators matched all 23 releases published during the incident to audit records and verified 62 package files against stored checksums. Hex does not log database reads, so it could not determine whether the attacker viewed email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets, sessions, or audit logs. It also could not fully rule out access to private packages or documentation. Investigators found no evidence of unauthorized database changes or lasting access. Hex replaced storage, email, and database credentials, among others, and changed the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. That forced users to sign in again. Hex advises users to change their passwords and reset two-factor authentication in Dashboard → Security. Under Authenticator App, select “Setup New App,” verify a code from the new entry, and save the new recovery codes. Check that links in emails claiming to come from Hex lead to hex.pm and forward suspicious messages to security@hex.pm. ElixirForum advises downloading packages only from repo.hex.pm and avoiding third-party mirrors until Hex releases clients with the new registry-signing system. Once available, Mix users can update using mix local.hex --force . Developers using rebar3 or Gleam should update those tools as well. Hex’s investigation also uncovered a related issue in Ash, fixed in version 3.38.0. Projects using db_connection should upgrade to 2.10.3 or later. items.title: Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR): Turning Sigma Alerts into ATT&CK-Mapped Attack Chains
items.summary: Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR) are correlation rules that sit one level above standard Sigma detections. Instead of matching a single log event, a Higher Order Sigma rule links the Sigma rules that fire on one host into an attack chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Most SOC teams already run hundreds of Sigma rules. Each flags one suspicious step, such as an encoded PowerShell command or a new service install, but analysts still have to work out which alerts belong to the same intrusion. HOSR moves that reasoning into the detection content itself, so multi-stage attack detection starts before anyone opens the alert queue. Contact Sales What Is Higher Order Sigma? Higher Order Sigma is a correlation layer for Sigma: rules whose inputs are the matches of other Sigma rules rather than raw events. SOC Prime introduced Higher Order Sigma rules in July 2026 and began a gradual rollout across its products. Each Higher Order Sigma rule is built around an Active Threat, SOC Prime’s curated intelligence item on a current campaign or malware family. The rule takes the detection rules attached to that threat and orders them using the threat’s Attack Flow, a sequence of adversary techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. The result describes how the whole attack unfolds, not just what one step looks like. The name echoes higher-order functions in programming, which take other functions as input. A standard Sigma rule asks whether a suspicious event happened. A Higher Order Sigma rule asks whether the steps of a known attack are happening together, on the same machine or same user, within a short time. In SOC Prime’s design, attack chains are authored by human experts as higher-order rules that correlate on ATT&CK techniques and on sequences of lower-level Sigma rules. Every rule is plain YAML, so detection engineers can read and review it like any other Sigma rule. How Does Standard Sigma Differ from Higher Order Sigma? A standard Sigma rule checks one event against field conditions. A Higher Order Sigma rule checks a sequence of Sigma matches against an attack’s expected progression. Standard Sigma is the vendor-agnostic YAML format detection engineers use to describe suspicious log events once and translate them to any SIEM, EDR, or data lake. The Sigma specification does offer correlation rules, such as event_count, value_count, temporal, and temporal_ordered, which group matches by a field within a timespan. Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR) are correlation rules that sit one level above standard Sigma detections. Instead of matching a single log event, a Higher Order Sigma rule links the Sigma rules that fire on one host into an attack chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

Most SOC teams already run hundreds of Sigma rules. Each flags one suspicious step, such as an encoded PowerShell command or a new service install, but analysts still have to work out which alerts belong to the same intrusion. HOSR moves that reasoning into the detection content itself, so multi-stage attack detection starts before anyone opens the alert queue.

Contact Sales

What Is Higher Order Sigma?

Higher Order Sigma is a correlation layer for Sigma: rules whose inputs are the matches of other Sigma rules rather than raw events. SOC Prime introduced Higher Order Sigma rules in July 2026 and began a gradual rollout across its products.

Each Higher Order Sigma rule is built around an Active Threat, SOC Prime’s curated intelligence item on a current campaign or malware family. The rule takes the detection rules attached to that threat and orders them using the threat’s Attack Flow, a sequence of adversary techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. The result describes how the whole attack unfolds, not just what one step looks like.

The name echoes higher-order functions in programming, which take other functions as input. A standard Sigma rule asks whether a suspicious event happened. A Higher Order Sigma rule asks whether the steps of a known attack are happening together, on the same machine or same user, within a short time.

In SOC Prime’s design, attack chains are authored by human experts as higher-order rules that correlate on ATT&CK techniques and on sequences of lower-level Sigma rules. Every rule is plain YAML, so detection engineers can read and review it like any other Sigma rule. 

How Does Standard Sigma Differ from Higher Order Sigma?

A standard Sigma rule checks one event against field conditions. A Higher Order Sigma rule checks a sequence of Sigma matches against an attack’s expected progression.

Standard Sigma is the vendor-agnostic YAML format detection engineers use to describe suspicious log events once and translate them to any SIEM, EDR, or data lake. Its strength is precision on a single log source. Its limit is that each rule sees one event in isolation, so ten related detections arrive as ten unrelated alerts.

The Sigma specification does offer correlation rules, such as event_count, value_count, temporal, and temporal_ordered, which group matches by a field within a timespan. They are useful, but each one is written by hand for a specific use case, and temporal types expect every referenced rule to match:

title: Admin share access followed by remote service install

correlation:

  type: temporal_ordered

  rules:

    – smb_admin_share_access

    – remote_service_creation

  group-by:

    – ComputerName

  timespan: 10m

If the attacker skips one step, a rule like this stays silent. Higher Order Sigma builds on the same correlation idea but is derived from threat intelligence, organized by ATT&CK stage, and designed to tolerate gaps.

AspectStandard Sigma ruleHigher Order Sigma ruleInputOne raw log eventEvents already tagged by Sigma rule matchesLogic sourceField conditions for one log sourceAttack Flow stages of an Active Threat, each backed by one or more Sigma rulesScopeA single eventMultiple events on the same host within a correlation windowMatchingExact: the condition is true or falsePartial: a chain forms once a set percentage of stages matchOutputA match tagged with ATT&CK technique and severityAn Attack Chain with match percentage, severity, and technique timelineWhere it runsSIEM, EDR, or pipeline queryCorrelation tier after Sigma tagging, in Prime Detect, Prime Hunt, and LogTotal

The two are complementary. Higher Order Sigma does not replace standard Sigma rules; it depends on them as building blocks.

What Are the Key Benefits for SOC Operations?

The main payoff is fewer, better alerts: analysts receive ATT&CK-mapped attack chains with context instead of isolated rule hits.

  • Less alert fatigue. Individual Sigma matches become tags, not alerts, and only correlated chains reach the queue. The funnel is steep: roughly 7% of raw events get tagged, and only a tiny fraction of those tagged events ever form an attack chain worth alerting on.
  • Fewer false positives. One noisy rule cannot create a chain on its own; it needs corroborating steps on the same host. An AI agent then classifies each chain as a confirmed detection or a likely false positive, and filtered-out chains are hidden by default.
  • Resilience to partial evasion. Because chains form at a match threshold, an attacker who skips a step or evades one rule can still be caught. At a 50% threshold, three of six stages are enough.
  • Faster triage. Each Attack Chain arrives with an AI summary, a technique timeline, and the matched rules, so analysts start from the full story instead of rebuilding it.
  • Less rule tuning. Because a single rule match no longer triggers an alert, noisy rules cost far less. Fine-tuning shifts from rewriting rules to adding context, which an AI agent can apply on top of the correlation output.
  • ATT&CK-aligned reporting. Every chain carries techniques, sub-techniques, and related threat actors, which feeds coverage reporting and threat-informed defense directly.
How Does Higher Order Sigma Work?

Higher Order Sigma is the second tier of a three-tier correlation process: Sigma rules tag events, Higher Order Sigma rules chain them, and an AI agent triages the result.

  1. Tier 1: Sigma rules tag events. In Prime Detect, Sigma rules run on streaming data before it reaches the SIEM, and each match carries an ATT&CK technique and a severity. In Prime Hunt, Sigma rules are translated into native queries and run against your Data Plane, whether SIEM, EDR/XDR, or data lake. Either way, a match marks an event as relevant; it is not yet an alert.
  2. Tier 2: Higher Order Sigma rules evaluate the sequence. Each rule maps to an Active Threat, and its stages follow that threat’s Attack Flow. A stage counts as matched when any of its underlying Sigma rules fires. Tagged events are grouped by host within the correlation window, and an Attack Chain forms once the matched stages reach the configured threshold.
  3. Tier 3: An AI agent triages the chain. The agent enriches the chain with context, analyzes the event sequence, and classifies it as a confirmed detection or a likely false positive.
  4. Analysts investigate and respond. Each chain moves through a status lifecycle, from New and Investigating to Confirmed or False Positive, then Resolved or Closed.

For example, imagine an Active Threat whose Attack Flow has six stages, from initial execution through credential dumping to lateral movement. With a 50% threshold, Sigma matches for any three of those stages on the same host, inside the correlation window, form an Attack Chain with a 50% match score. A single matching stage stays a quiet tag.

The same correlation powers LogTotal, SOC Prime’s tool for investigating logs during an incident. It matches exported logs against detection rules, then uses Higher Order Sigma rules and agentic AI to return ranked attack chains.

Conclusion

Higher Order Sigma Rules shift detection from “what happened” to “which attack is in progress.” For SOC teams, that means fewer and richer alerts, ATT&CK-mapped attack chains, and detection logic that tolerates gaps. To explore them, open any Active Threat on the SOC Prime Platform and check its Higher Order Sigma tab, or filter Advanced Search by Higher Order Sigma.
