items.title: Pluralistic: New York vs auto-enshittification (25 Nov 2026)
items.summary: Today's links New York vs auto-enshittification : A blueprint for states to fix Congress's mistake. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : Homebrew DRM; HTML v regexp; Tesla-financial complex; Spain v Wall St landlords; "Cooking in Maximum Security." Upcoming appearances : Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal, Sheffield. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. New York vs auto-enshittification ( permalink ) As of February 27, 2027, it will be illegal for companies in New York to charge car-owners a subscription fee or an upcharge for any software feature that runs on hardware already installed in their car. It's a bold – if imperfect – disenshittification gambit aimed at the extremely (and increasingly) enshittified automotive industry: https://wgna.com/car-bill-extra-fees/ In a state of nature, there'd be no reason to pass a law like this. Say BMW decided to sell you a car that charged you a monthly subscription for the "feature" that auto-dipped your high-beams when there was an oncoming car (a thing BMW actually does): https://www.autoevolution.com/news/netizens-up-in-arms-over-bmw-adaptive-headlight-subscription-237335.html In a state of nature, BMW's sleazy scam would conjure forth competitors who would offer mechanics and drivers a one-click way to unlock the feature forever. Drivers would curse BMW and pay a one-time fee to get permanent access to the feature, and that would be the end of the matter. Indeed, the fact that this third-party fix could exist at all might well convince BMW not to bother with the high-beam scam in the first place (and if it didn't, well, then tinkerers, hackers, and entrepreneurs would swiftly obviate it). But we don't live in a state of nature. We live in a world with a federal "anticircumvention" law: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA 1201), which imposes a 5-year sentence and a $500k fine for this kind of reverse engineering, even if it does not result in a copyright infringement. There's no copyright law that says you can't change the software in your car to activate your high-beams' automatic controller, but that doesn't matter, because activating the controller without BMW's permission requires a reverse-engineering step and that's a felony. Jay Freeman rightly calls this "felony contempt of business model" because it lets companies send you to literal prison for doing otherwise legal things, just because it makes them unhappy. What's more, copyright is a firmly federal matter: copyright law "pre-empts" the states, meaning that states can't pass laws that modify federal copyright policy. That means that states can't override DMCA 1201 by legalizing reverse-engineering for otherwise lawful purposes (such as independent repair, performing software upgrades, or allowing generic consumables and parts). Anticircumvention is an attractive nuisance: it invites manufacturers to dream up as many scams as they can think of and then bury them in their products, secure in the knowledge that it is a literal felony to thwart their commercial plans. It's especially bad for cars, where anticircumvention is used: to block third-party parts and independent repair; to prevent drivers from preventing manufacturers, lenders and dealerships from spying on their driving habits, car informatics, and locations; to enable lenders (and hackers who break into dealerships' computers) to immobilize your car without any notice, appeal or due process: https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/24/rent-to-pwn/#kitt-is-a-demon The New York State bill (S.9348A/A.10411A) partially addresses some of these unfair and deceptive practices: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9348/amendment/A Before I get into what this law does (and doesn't) do, I want to get into how it does anything at all . Remember: anticircumvention was shoehorned into copyright law, and copyright is a federal matter. Copyright enjoys pre-emption, a ban on states' modifying it. At first blush, it seems like the states shouldn't be able to do anything about the enshittification that anticircumvention law enables. But the Right to Repair movement came up with a clever hack around pre-emption. States can't override federal copyright law, but state legislatures can regulate goods and services that are sold within their states. That means that states can simply ban the sale of goods that use anticircumvention to rip off or spy on the people who live within state limits. This is the basis for several successful Right to Repair laws, starting in 2022 with Colorado's powered wheelchair repair law (HB22-1031, cosponsored by the very excellent Brianna Titone): https://pluralistic.net/2022/06/08/chair-ish/#r2r This law does not purport to limit which copyrights the private-equity-backed powered wheelchair duopoly can exercise. It just orders anyone selling powered wheelchairs in Colorado to take steps to enable independent repair such that these copyright issues (including anticircumvention) never arise. This became the template for a slew of state repair bills, including Oregon's electronics repair law, which was later copy/pasted into Washington state law: https://pirg.org/oregon/updates/governor-kotek-signs-the-right-to-repair-act-into-law/ A very similar law was passed in New York state, only to be gutted by Governor Kathy Hochul: https://www.techdirt.com/2024/02/07/nys-right-to-repair-law-was-neutered-by-lobbyists-and-governor-hochul-after-passage-now-some-lawmakers-are-trying-to-fix-it/ Hochul will shortly get a chance to redeem herself, when A8405, a law that re-inserts all the provisions she stripped out of the original repair law, comes to her desk: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/A8405 Perhaps Hochul will sign that law. After all, her press release about the new automotive bill sure makes it sound like she's anti-enshittification: My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets. https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/money-your-pockets-governor-hochul-signs-bill-restricting-exploitative-vehicle-subscription But the specifics of this new NY automotive bill matter, and they're a decidedly mixed bag. Let's start with the penalty for noncompliance: a dealer, automotive manufacturer or lender who violates the new law faces a whopping $250 fine per violation. In this case, a dealer who manages to fleece one driver for every three who know their rights and can figure out how to enforce them will still come out ahead – and that's only if you can get the dealer to refund your $1000, which might involve going to small claims court. Then there's the carve-outs: this law does not cover subscription fees and software upsells for "navigation system updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle wi-fi, telematics services, roadside assistance, software-dependent driver assistance or driver automation features, or vehicle-connected services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This is a huge loophole. Take that last clause, "services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This clause allows manufacturers to bypass the entire statute, merely by redesigning their subscription and software upsells to "rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." For example, the BMW feature that automatically dips your high-beams could "require" a daily check for new versions and then the company can claim that the feature relies "on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." Sure, a judge might eventually find that "continued operation" doesn't mean a daily check for software updates, but only after the state AG or a class action lawyer forces the question, which could take years. Also: don't hold your breath waiting for the class action lawyer, because the car manufacturers can also make you click through a binding arbitration waiver when you first turn on your car and thus take away your right to join a class action: https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/27/shit-shack/#binding-arbitration Beyond this, there's the breadth of vague phrases like "driver automation features" (is automatically dipping your high-beams a "driver automation feature?" I could sure see a lawyer making that argument). Likewise "telematics" (a buzzword that might mean anything, nothing or everything). On the other hand, there are some interesting ambiguities in this bill that I quite like. For example: if you live in New Jersey, but you happen to be in New York on the day Tesla bills you for subscribing to your whole battery (some Tesla models only let you use half your battery's charge unless you pay a monthly fee). Does that mean Tesla violated the law by charging a fee for a subscription feature for a car that is in the state of New York? That would be a fun one to see! It won't stop your car from spying on you and ratting you out to your insurer: https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars It won't help you if the manufacturer goes bust and bricks your car: https://pluralistic.net/2024/10/10/software-based-car/#based It won't help you if Tesla hacks your odometer to sell a lie about the range you can expect from your charge: https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/28/edison-not-tesla/#demon-haunted-world This law would have had much more effect if it was better-drafted; on the other hand, maybe if it was drafted to capture a more meaningful slice of enshittificatory gambits, Hochul would have gutted it the way she did with the state's 2022 electronics repair bill. Above all, though, we must remember: the only reason this bill exists at all is that Congress created DMCA 1201, the "felony contempt of business-model" law that lets companies conjure new crimes out of thin air and send you to prison for making their shareholders sad. It's fantastic that the Repair Coalition came up with a loophole that lets states protect the American public from some of the worst effects of anticircumvention law, and it's cool that this tactic is being used to fight other kinds of enshittification. But none of this should be necessary at all , and the real fix is for Congress to repeal Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. New York vs auto-enshittification (permalink)

As of February 27, 2027, it will be illegal for companies in New York to charge car-owners a subscription fee or an upcharge for any software feature that runs on hardware already installed in their car. It's a bold – if imperfect – disenshittification gambit aimed at the extremely (and increasingly) enshittified automotive industry:

https://wgna.com/car-bill-extra-fees/

In a state of nature, there'd be no reason to pass a law like this. Say BMW decided to sell you a car that charged you a monthly subscription for the "feature" that auto-dipped your high-beams when there was an oncoming car (a thing BMW actually does):

https://www.autoevolution.com/news/netizens-up-in-arms-over-bmw-adaptive-headlight-subscription-237335.html

In a state of nature, BMW's sleazy scam would conjure forth competitors who would offer mechanics and drivers a one-click way to unlock the feature forever. Drivers would curse BMW and pay a one-time fee to get permanent access to the feature, and that would be the end of the matter. Indeed, the fact that this third-party fix could exist at all might well convince BMW not to bother with the high-beam scam in the first place (and if it didn't, well, then tinkerers, hackers, and entrepreneurs would swiftly obviate it).

But we don't live in a state of nature. We live in a world with a federal "anticircumvention" law: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA 1201), which imposes a 5-year sentence and a $500k fine for this kind of reverse engineering, even if it does not result in a copyright infringement.

There's no copyright law that says you can't change the software in your car to activate your high-beams' automatic controller, but that doesn't matter, because activating the controller without BMW's permission requires a reverse-engineering step and that's a felony.

Jay Freeman rightly calls this "felony contempt of business model" because it lets companies send you to literal prison for doing otherwise legal things, just because it makes them unhappy.

What's more, copyright is a firmly federal matter: copyright law "pre-empts" the states, meaning that states can't pass laws that modify federal copyright policy. That means that states can't override DMCA 1201 by legalizing reverse-engineering for otherwise lawful purposes (such as independent repair, performing software upgrades, or allowing generic consumables and parts).

Anticircumvention is an attractive nuisance: it invites manufacturers to dream up as many scams as they can think of and then bury them in their products, secure in the knowledge that it is a literal felony to thwart their commercial plans. It's especially bad for cars, where anticircumvention is used:

  • to block third-party parts and independent repair;

  • to prevent drivers from preventing manufacturers, lenders and dealerships from spying on their driving habits, car informatics, and locations;

  • to enable lenders (and hackers who break into dealerships' computers) to immobilize your car without any notice, appeal or due process:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/24/rent-to-pwn/#kitt-is-a-demon

The New York State bill (S.9348A/A.10411A) partially addresses some of these unfair and deceptive practices:

https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9348/amendment/A

Before I get into what this law does (and doesn't) do, I want to get into how it does anything at all. Remember: anticircumvention was shoehorned into copyright law, and copyright is a federal matter. Copyright enjoys pre-emption, a ban on states' modifying it.

At first blush, it seems like the states shouldn't be able to do anything about the enshittification that anticircumvention law enables. But the Right to Repair movement came up with a clever hack around pre-emption. States can't override federal copyright law, but state legislatures can regulate goods and services that are sold within their states. That means that states can simply ban the sale of goods that use anticircumvention to rip off or spy on the people who live within state limits.

This is the basis for several successful Right to Repair laws, starting in 2022 with Colorado's powered wheelchair repair law (HB22-1031, cosponsored by the very excellent Brianna Titone):

https://pluralistic.net/2022/06/08/chair-ish/#r2r

This law does not purport to limit which copyrights the private-equity-backed powered wheelchair duopoly can exercise. It just orders anyone selling powered wheelchairs in Colorado to take steps to enable independent repair such that these copyright issues (including anticircumvention) never arise.

This became the template for a slew of state repair bills, including Oregon's electronics repair law, which was later copy/pasted into Washington state law:

https://pirg.org/oregon/updates/governor-kotek-signs-the-right-to-repair-act-into-law/

A very similar law was passed in New York state, only to be gutted by Governor Kathy Hochul:

https://www.techdirt.com/2024/02/07/nys-right-to-repair-law-was-neutered-by-lobbyists-and-governor-hochul-after-passage-now-some-lawmakers-are-trying-to-fix-it/

Hochul will shortly get a chance to redeem herself, when A8405, a law that re-inserts all the provisions she stripped out of the original repair law, comes to her desk:

https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/A8405

Perhaps Hochul will sign that law. After all, her press release about the new automotive bill sure makes it sound like she's anti-enshittification:

My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.

https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/money-your-pockets-governor-hochul-signs-bill-restricting-exploitative-vehicle-subscription

But the specifics of this new NY automotive bill matter, and they're a decidedly mixed bag. Let's start with the penalty for noncompliance: a dealer, automotive manufacturer or lender who violates the new law faces a whopping $250 fine per violation. That means that if your dealer charges you $1,000 for a software upgrade and you later realize you've been ripped off, they'll only pay a penalty of $250.

In this case, a dealer who manages to fleece one driver for every three who know their rights and can figure out how to enforce them will still come out ahead – and that's only if you can get the dealer to refund your $1000, which might involve going to small claims court.

Then there's the carve-outs: this law does not cover subscription fees and software upsells for "navigation system updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle wi-fi, telematics services, roadside assistance, software-dependent driver assistance or driver automation features, or vehicle-connected services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation."

This is a huge loophole. Take that last clause, "services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This clause allows manufacturers to bypass the entire statute, merely by redesigning their subscription and software upsells to "rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." For example, the BMW feature that automatically dips your high-beams could "require" a daily check for new versions and then the company can claim that the feature relies "on cellular or other data networks for continued operation."

Sure, a judge might eventually find that "continued operation" doesn't mean a daily check for software updates, but only after the state AG or a class action lawyer forces the question, which could take years. Also: don't hold your breath waiting for the class action lawyer, because the car manufacturers can also make you click through a binding arbitration waiver when you first turn on your car and thus take away your right to join a class action:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/27/shit-shack/#binding-arbitration

Beyond this, there's the breadth of vague phrases like "driver automation features" (is automatically dipping your high-beams a "driver automation feature?" I could sure see a lawyer making that argument). Likewise "telematics" (a buzzword that might mean anything, nothing or everything).

On the other hand, there are some interesting ambiguities in this bill that I quite like. For example: if you live in New Jersey, but you happen to be in New York on the day Tesla bills you for subscribing to your whole battery (some Tesla models only let you use half your battery's charge unless you pay a monthly fee). Does that mean Tesla violated the law by charging a fee for a subscription feature for a car that is in the state of New York? That would be a fun one to see!

Like I said, this is only a partial fix for auto-enshittification. It won't stop your car from spying on you and ratting you out to your insurer:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars

It won't help you if the manufacturer goes bust and bricks your car:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/10/10/software-based-car/#based

It won't help you if Tesla hacks your odometer to sell a lie about the range you can expect from your charge:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/28/edison-not-tesla/#demon-haunted-world

This law would have had much more effect if it was better-drafted; on the other hand, maybe if it was drafted to capture a more meaningful slice of enshittificatory gambits, Hochul would have gutted it the way she did with the state's 2022 electronics repair bill.

Above all, though, we must remember: the only reason this bill exists at all is that Congress created DMCA 1201, the "felony contempt of business-model" law that lets companies conjure new crimes out of thin air and send you to prison for making their shareholders sad.

It's fantastic that the Repair Coalition came up with a loophole that lets states protect the American public from some of the worst effects of anticircumvention law, and it's cool that this tactic is being used to fight other kinds of enshittification.

But none of this should be necessary at all, and the real fix is for Congress to repeal Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

items.summary_html:
An open source adventure featuring Kubernetes, agent-substrate, kagent, AI agents, drones, and more!

Just 30 seconds before going live for the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 closing keynote, “Cloud Native Without Limits: What Can AI Agents Do for Us?”, while Abdel Sghiouar was introducing me, Cory Jett leaned over and whispered: “The drone isn’t connecting to the controller!” 😱

A heart-stopping moment!

Thankfully, a quick reboot saved the day. And then came the moment I’ll never forget: walking onto the stage with a live drone following right behind me! 🚁✨

And when I finally walked off stage, all the nervousness and anxiety were gone. I was just SO happy! What a feeling! ❤️

On-stage live demo with the drone and big screens

🥋 From Amsterdam to Salt Lake City: Never give up!

After my Amsterdam keynote, where the drone camera failed, Christian Dussol taught me the martial arts lesson of “Osu” (never give up! 🥋💪). That lesson stuck with me, and I wanted to push the boundaries even further in Salt Lake City.

Striking the “Osu” posture after the Amsterdam keynote

While brainstorming with Allison Price around our theme, “Cloud Native Without Limits,” we asked ourselves: What if we could let the audience experience what it’s like to fly and build something live on stage, powered by AI agents?

Of course, bringing a live drone indoors isn’t exactly plug-and-play. There was quite a bit of work behind the scenes!

🛠️ Behind the scenes: Making the impossible possible

A few challenges we had to tackle:

🛩️ Regulatory compliance: Back in August, we learned that an FAA Part 107-certified remote pilot was required for our indoor drone operation. Cory stepped up, completed the necessary training in just one week, and saved the demo! 🙌

Teaser at the venue 😅

🏠 Home testing: I got propeller guards so I could safely experiment with code, test flight paths, and practice flying indoors at home. Let’s just say my house became a mini drone testing lab!

Flight testing at home with propeller guards

But this demo was about much more than flying a drone. We wanted to show what real-time agentic execution looks like, with the right guardrails, sandboxing, and observability in place.

🤖 Under the hood: The Cloud Native technologies behind the drone

Here’s what powered the experience:

🤖 Agents: Running on CNCF Sanbox projects agent-substrate, and kagent providing an opinionated layer for building and running agents.

🔐Then AAIF Growth project agentgateway: Playing multiple roles:

  • LLM gateway: Rate limiting and controlling access to models.
  • Egress gateway (as part of agent-substrate): Enforcing sandbox and network access policies.
  • MCP gateway: Handling authentication and authorization for Model Context Protocol tool calls with an Identity Provider, for example, Keycloak.

📊 OpenTelemetry and Jaeger: Providing end-to-end observability across agent execution through agentgateway and agent-substrate, including rate-limiting errors, the duration of each tool call, and where agents spend most of their time.

All coming together to make an AI-powered physical experience happen, live on stage!

The moment when it all comes together live on stage

💜 A big Thank You & what’s next? 🇪🇸

The community’s response was incredible! It’s exciting to see how far we’ve come as an industry, bringing AI models, agentic AI, and cloud native technologies together to make things possible that would have seemed like science fiction just a few years ago.

A massive THANK YOU to my manager, Idit Levine, for her unwavering support; Cory Jett, for making the drone flight possible; Allison Price, for brainstorming this adventure with me; Jonathan Bryce, for loving the drone idea when I casually brought it up during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2025; Elna Vogel, for making sure we had the required insurance.

And of course, a huge shout-out to the entire event and technical teams who helped bring this adventure to life! ❤️

Last but definitely not least, THANK YOU to the agent-substrate, kagent, and agentgateway communities! They answered every question I threw at them, responded incredibly quickly, and were always ready to jump in and debug live if needed. I couldn’t have pulled this off without you! 💜

My #substrate-dev team CNCF slack

📺 Missed the keynote? Catch the full recording!

Now, I’m officially wrapping up the Drone 2 chapter and already looking forward to building something fresh for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2027 in Barcelona! 🇪🇸

So, what physical objects or hardware should we hack on next? Drones have had their moment. What’s next? What could we build that I haven’t even imagined yet? 🙂

items.title: Agents you didn’t deploy can still read your data
items.summary: On October 15, India’s national CERT, CERT-In, issued a critical advisory. AI agents that AI model providers were running during research and evaluation had reached the live systems of Indian organizations and read business records, including personal data and confidential material. None of the affected organizations detected it. Every case came to light because the providers disclosed it after their own review. Source: CERT-In, advisory CIAD-2026-0049 , Oct. 2026. Two weeks later, on October 30, Chainalysis disclosed that it had detected an external actor using “offensive agentic techniques” to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools. It found no indication that investigation content, clear-text passwords, MFA secrets, or session tokens were accessed. Some customer account details, such as user IDs, names, and email addresses, were accessed. Source: Chainalysis, Security Incident Information , Oct. 2026. Neither case involved an agent the victim deployed. Controls built around your own agents don’t reach agents someone else is running. Part 1: Finding it a day later isn’t protecting it Part 2: Most agents reach sensitive data with no verified DLP What the vendors say PKWARE’s earlier series, “The Data, Not the Agent,” covered BigID and Varonis. Here is what five more vendors say in their own published material, paraphrased and dated. Vendor and month What it says it does for AI agents Cyera, Aug. 2026 Agent Guardian inventories agents across endpoints, SaaS, and cloud, including shadow agents and MCP servers, and maps the data each can reach. Cyera Endpoint extends the controls to devices. Securiti, Feb. 2026 Agent Commander, introduced with Veeam, detects AI risk, applies runtime guardrails, and can roll back what an agent did. Immuta, Mar. 2026 Agentic Data Access gives agents their own identity, attributes, intent, and audit trail, and grants access when it is needed instead of as standing privilege. OneTrust, Sept. 2026 CORIE enforces enterprise policy at runtime while agents work, and records their decisions. Informatica, May 2026 Agent Fabric Context Catalog: one place to discover, govern, and operate data assets and AI agents together. Read the verbs Inventory. Detect. Monitor. Govern. Enforce. Roll back. Every claim in the table is about the agent, the identity behind it, or the session it runs in. That is real work, and these are serious platforms. But Cyera’s own release describes shadow agents and MCP servers that security teams did not know existed, and CERT-In’s advisory describes agents run by someone else, which none of the affected organizations detected. The other side of the argument Most of the field is fencing the agent. We fence the data. CERT-In says these agents got in using credentials left in application configuration and public code repositories, and cloud roles with too much access. A credential like that opens what that identity can open. It doesn’t come with a key unless that identity was given one. Protection on the data changes what they find. When PK Protect encrypts a supported file, the protection stays on the file after it moves. PK Protect’s key management issues the keys, and your directory groups decide who can use them. An agent that hasn’t been given a key can reach the file and still can’t read it. On supported databases, warehouses, and cloud storage, sensitive values are masked, so there is nothing to unlock. Adding more agents doesn’t change the protection on the data. PK Protect doesn’t inventory agents or monitor their intent. The vendors above do. How that fits with protection on the data, for agents with their own identity and for assistants working on a person’s behalf, is in Part 2 of “The Data, Not the Agent.” You can’t govern every agent. You can decide what they find. Four questions for any AI security pitch The pitch (paraphrased) Ask this We inventory every agent. What protects the data that an agent we missed can reach? We enforce policy at runtime. What happens to the file when the policy is not in the path, or fails? Agents get least-privilege access. Is the file still protected after an authorized agent copies it somewhere? One control plane for people, machines, and agents. Can the same platform encrypt, mask, or redact the data, or does it report on it? Request your assessment

items.title: Introducing context-aware rules for AWS Network Firewall
items.summary: AWS Network Firewall now supports context-aware rules , which match traffic by the AWS resources that send and receive it instead of by IP address. A rule can name a virtual private cloud (VPC), a subnet, a security group, or a transit gateway attachment. Rules that match on IP addresses have to keep up with every workload that scales out, is replaced, or moves. Short-lived workloads are the hardest to keep up with. items.title: Introducing AWS Network Firewall Next Generation policy
items.summary: When it comes to inspecting network traffic, many security teams want two things from a firewall. They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats. Today, you can do both with AWS Network Firewall , a stateful, managed network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service. In a Classic policy , your access rules and your threat rules run together in one stateful engine and share one rule capacity. With Next Generation policies , access control and threat protection each get their own engine in the same firewall. A firewall engine allows the traffic you approve and drops the rest. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) engine checks the allowed traffic with AWS managed rule groups or with rules that you write. Each engine has its own rule capacity , so adding access rules doesn’t take capacity away from threat protection. In this post, we walk through what Next Generation policies are, how they evaluate traffic, and the new concepts they introduce. We use sample records to cover what each engine logs and how to validate a policy with the new monitor mode. To put it all together, we walk through creating an example Next Generation policy. How a Next Generation policy works A Next Generation policy inspects traffic with two engines , in sequence. Traffic that the firewall engine allows moves to the IPS engine, and traffic that the firewall engine blocks goes no further. The firewall engine is drop by default, and the IPS engine is pass by default. If you already write Suricata rules, the two engines will feel familiar. The firewall engine is built on Suricata 8 firewall mode , which follows each connection as it progresses and evaluates rules at each step. The IPS engine uses the Suricata compatible intrusion detection system (IDS) and IPS rules that you already know from the stateful engine in a Classic policy, with one difference: it evaluates rules in action order and doesn’t support Classic options such as strict order. A Classic policy uses a stateless engine and then a stateful engine that evaluates access rules and threat rules together. In a Next Generation policy, both engines are stateful, so each rule is evaluated with full connection context, which helps keep traffic handling consistent and predictable. The firewall engine works up to the application layer. It follows each connection for its entire flow, from the first packet through the TCP handshake and application layer exchanges such as the TLS client hello, and evaluates your access rules along the way (Figure 1). Figure 1: Classic and Next Generation policy engines and their rule capacity. This separation changes how you design a policy. Because each engine has one job, you can plan access control and threat protection on their own, and different teams can work independently. For example, a networking team can manage access rules while a security team handles threat detection, and neither has to rewrite the other’s rules. The firewall engine controls access You configure access control by specifying an action for a protocol, along with a source and destination. Rules run in the order that you set . Traffic that no rule allows gets the policy’s firewall default action , which is drop unless you change it. In a Next Generation policy, the drop default action applies from the first packet, so for TCP traffic the firewall can drop the initial SYN. Unlike the drop established default action in a Classic policy, it doesn’t wait for a connection to be established. A few terms explain how the firewall engine evaluates traffic. Connection states are the protocol states that a connection progresses through, such as the TCP handshake and the TLS client hello. A hook is the point at a connection state where your rules attach, so a rule’s hook sets when the firewall engine evaluates it. Each rule also has an action , such as accept, drop, or reject. Its action scope sets how much of the traffic the action applies to, from one packet or one transaction up to the whole connection, called the flow . For more details, see Firewall engine hooks . When you build a rule in the console, you choose a protocol and then two settings: Connection state , which sets the rule’s hook, and Action scope . For example, to allow a domain over TLS, you match its server name at the Client Hello connection state with the This flow action scope. Because the firewall engine is drop by default, a connection advances to the next connection state only while your rules keep accepting it. For example, a connection can pass the TCP handshake and still be dropped at the TLS client hello. That happens when its server name isn’t on your approved list (Figure 2). Figure 2: A connection is accepted at the TCP handshake hook and dropped at the TLS client hello hook. In Figure 2, the rule for www.amazon.com accepts the flow when it matches the server name at the TLS client hello hook. No rule accepts example.com at that hook, so the firewall default action drops it. You don’t have to write every rule in raw Suricata syntax. You can build rules in the console rule builder, or, as in the example later in this post, enter your domains in a domain list rule group, and Network Firewall builds the rules for you. Action scope also sets where an accepted connection goes next. An accept with the hook scope allows the connection to advance to the next connection state, where the rules at that hook evaluate it. An accept with the flow scope lets the connection skip the remaining hooks and move to the IPS engine (Figure 3). A firewall rule can also bypass the IPS engine for specific traffic when you choose. For the valid combinations of action and scope at each type of hook, see Firewall engine actions and scopes . Figure 3: An accept with the hook scope compared with an accept with the flow scope. The IPS engine looks for threats Traffic that the firewall engine allows then reaches the IPS engine , which inspects it with Suricata compatible rules. The IPS engine is designed to look for specific threats, so it blocks only traffic that matches a threat rule. IPS rules evaluate in action order . Pass rules go first, then drop, reject, and alert rules, regardless of the order in which you define them. For the full path through both engines, see How Network Firewall filters traffic with a Next Generation policy . We recommend that you start with the AWS managed rule groups . Because the IPS engine is built on the industry standard Suricata engine, you can also run Suricata compatible rule sets from specialized security providers, alongside rules that you write yourself. Referenced rule groups and embedded rules Each engine gets its rules from its own section of the policy . You can add rules in two ways and mix both in one section. Referenced rule groups are separate resources, and they’re the only kind of rule group that Classic policies support. You create a rule group once and add it to as many policies as you need. You can also share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) . For details, see Sharing AWS Network Firewall resources . When you update the rule group, each policy that references it picks up the change. You set a referenced rule group’s capacity when you create it, and you can’t change it afterward, so leave room for it to grow. Embedded rules are new with Next Generation policies. You write them directly inside one policy, and they belong to that policy only, so you can’t share them with another policy. Use them to add rules quickly that are specific to that policy. They use that engine’s rule capacity, and you don’t set a capacity up front. Embedded rules in both engine sections share a combined limit. For all limits, see AWS Network Firewall quotas . Read what each engine logs Whichever way you add rules, both engines write to the same alert and flow logs, which you configure in the logging configuration . Each alert record carries new fields that show which engine wrote it and, for the firewall engine, the hook where the decision happened. The following record came from a test, in enforce mode, of the example policy that you build later in this post. A host tried to reach example.com, which isn’t on the allow list. { "firewall_name": "example-fw", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event_timestamp": "1794341434", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "app_proto": "tls", "src_ip": "10.0.1.25", "src_port": 42698, "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "tls": { "sni": "example.com" }, "alert": { "engine": "fw", "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 2201001, "signature": "SURICATA FW default app policy", "severity": 3 }, "firewall": { "hook": "tls:client_hello", "policy": "drop:flow,alert" }, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "aws_metadata": { "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy" }, "timestamp": "2026-11-10T20:10:34.141643+0000" } } The following table explains the key fields in this record. Field Value What it tells you alert.engine fw The firewall engine wrote this record. firewall.hook tls:client_hello The decision happened at the TLS client hello, where the client sends the server name example.com. alert.signature SURICATA FW default app policy No rule matched, so the firewall default action applied. The default action logs its drops on its own, so you don’t need an alert rule to see what it blocks. firewall.policy drop:flow,alert The action and scope that applied. The default action dropped the whole flow and wrote an alert. aws_metadata.resource_arn arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy The policy itself is the source, because the record doesn’t come from one of your rule groups. When a connection that the firewall engine allowed matches a threat rule, the IPS engine writes its own record. In this test, the firewall engine allowed TLS to one test server by IP address. The IPS section also held the following embedded rule, which drops TLS connections with a JA4 fingerprint that your threat intelligence flags. The fingerprint in this rule is a sample value: drop tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"; flow:to_server,established; ja4.hash; content:"t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb"; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:900002; rev:1;) This is a sample rule to show the IPS engine at work. In your own policies, we recommend that you start with the AWS managed threat signature rule groups and add custom rules where you need them. When it comes to inspecting network traffic, many security teams want two things from a firewall. They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats. Today, you can do both with AWS Network Firewall, a stateful, managed network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service. In a Classic policy, your access rules and your threat rules run together in one stateful engine and share one rule capacity.

With Next Generation policies, access control and threat protection each get their own engine in the same firewall. A firewall engine allows the traffic you approve and drops the rest. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) engine checks the allowed traffic with AWS managed rule groups or with rules that you write. Each engine has its own rule capacity, so adding access rules doesn’t take capacity away from threat protection.

In this post, we walk through what Next Generation policies are, how they evaluate traffic, and the new concepts they introduce. We use sample records to cover what each engine logs and how to validate a policy with the new monitor mode. To put it all together, we walk through creating an example Next Generation policy.

How a Next Generation policy works

A Next Generation policy inspects traffic with two engines, in sequence. Traffic that the firewall engine allows moves to the IPS engine, and traffic that the firewall engine blocks goes no further. The firewall engine is drop by default, and the IPS engine is pass by default.

If you already write Suricata rules, the two engines will feel familiar. The firewall engine is built on Suricata 8 firewall mode, which follows each connection as it progresses and evaluates rules at each step. The IPS engine uses the Suricata compatible intrusion detection system (IDS) and IPS rules that you already know from the stateful engine in a Classic policy, with one difference: it evaluates rules in action order and doesn’t support Classic options such as strict order.

A Classic policy uses a stateless engine and then a stateful engine that evaluates access rules and threat rules together. In a Next Generation policy, both engines are stateful, so each rule is evaluated with full connection context, which helps keep traffic handling consistent and predictable. The firewall engine works up to the application layer. It follows each connection for its entire flow, from the first packet through the TCP handshake and application layer exchanges such as the TLS client hello, and evaluates your access rules along the way (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Classic and Next Generation policy engines and their rule capacity.

This separation changes how you design a policy. Because each engine has one job, you can plan access control and threat protection on their own, and different teams can work independently. For example, a networking team can manage access rules while a security team handles threat detection, and neither has to rewrite the other’s rules.

The firewall engine controls access

You configure access control by specifying an action for a protocol, along with a source and destination. Rules run in the order that you set. Traffic that no rule allows gets the policy’s firewall default action, which is drop unless you change it. In a Next Generation policy, the drop default action applies from the first packet, so for TCP traffic the firewall can drop the initial SYN. Unlike the drop established default action in a Classic policy, it doesn’t wait for a connection to be established.

A few terms explain how the firewall engine evaluates traffic. Connection states are the protocol states that a connection progresses through, such as the TCP handshake and the TLS client hello. A hook is the point at a connection state where your rules attach, so a rule’s hook sets when the firewall engine evaluates it. Each rule also has an action, such as accept, drop, or reject. Its action scope sets how much of the traffic the action applies to, from one packet or one transaction up to the whole connection, called the flow. For more details, see Firewall engine hooks.

When you build a rule in the console, you choose a protocol and then two settings: Connection state, which sets the rule’s hook, and Action scope. For example, to allow a domain over TLS, you match its server name at the Client Hello connection state with the This flow action scope.

Because the firewall engine is drop by default, a connection advances to the next connection state only while your rules keep accepting it. For example, a connection can pass the TCP handshake and still be dropped at the TLS client hello. That happens when its server name isn’t on your approved list (Figure 2).

Figure 2: A connection is accepted at the TCP handshake hook and dropped at the TLS client hello hook.

In Figure 2, the rule for www.amazon.com accepts the flow when it matches the server name at the TLS client hello hook. No rule accepts example.com at that hook, so the firewall default action drops it.

You don’t have to write every rule in raw Suricata syntax. You can build rules in the console rule builder, or, as in the example later in this post, enter your domains in a domain list rule group, and Network Firewall builds the rules for you.

Action scope also sets where an accepted connection goes next. An accept with the hook scope allows the connection to advance to the next connection state, where the rules at that hook evaluate it. An accept with the flow scope lets the connection skip the remaining hooks and move to the IPS engine (Figure 3). A firewall rule can also bypass the IPS engine for specific traffic when you choose. For the valid combinations of action and scope at each type of hook, see Firewall engine actions and scopes.

Figure 3: An accept with the hook scope compared with an accept with the flow scope.

The IPS engine looks for threats

Traffic that the firewall engine allows then reaches the IPS engine, which inspects it with Suricata compatible rules. The IPS engine is designed to look for specific threats, so it blocks only traffic that matches a threat rule. IPS rules evaluate in action order. Pass rules go first, then drop, reject, and alert rules, regardless of the order in which you define them. For the full path through both engines, see How Network Firewall filters traffic with a Next Generation policy.

We recommend that you start with the AWS managed rule groups. Because the IPS engine is built on the industry standard Suricata engine, you can also run Suricata compatible rule sets from specialized security providers, alongside rules that you write yourself.

Referenced rule groups and embedded rules

Each engine gets its rules from its own section of the policy. You can add rules in two ways and mix both in one section.

Referenced rule groups are separate resources, and they’re the only kind of rule group that Classic policies support. You create a rule group once and add it to as many policies as you need. You can also share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). For details, see Sharing AWS Network Firewall resources. When you update the rule group, each policy that references it picks up the change. You set a referenced rule group’s capacity when you create it, and you can’t change it afterward, so leave room for it to grow.

Embedded rules are new with Next Generation policies. You write them directly inside one policy, and they belong to that policy only, so you can’t share them with another policy. Use them to add rules quickly that are specific to that policy. They use that engine’s rule capacity, and you don’t set a capacity up front. Embedded rules in both engine sections share a combined limit. For all limits, see AWS Network Firewall quotas.

Read what each engine logs

Whichever way you add rules, both engines write to the same alert and flow logs, which you configure in the logging configuration. Each alert record carries new fields that show which engine wrote it and, for the firewall engine, the hook where the decision happened.

The following record came from a test, in enforce mode, of the example policy that you build later in this post. A host tried to reach example.com, which isn’t on the allow list.

  "firewall_name": "example-fw",
  "availability_zone": "us-east-1a",
  "event_timestamp": "1794341434",
  "event": {
    "event_type": "alert",
    "app_proto": "tls",
    "src_ip": "10.0.1.25",
    "src_port": 42698,
    "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10",
    "dest_port": 443,
    "proto": "TCP",
    "tls": {
      "sni": "example.com"
    },
    "alert": {
      "engine": "fw",
      "action": "blocked",
      "signature_id": 2201001,
      "signature": "SURICATA FW default app policy",
      "severity": 3
    },
    "firewall": {
      "hook": "tls:client_hello",
      "policy": "drop:flow,alert"
    },
    "verdict": {
      "action": "drop"
    },
    "aws_metadata": {
      "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy"
    },

The default action logs its drops on its own, so you don’t need an alert rule to see what it blocks. firewall.policy drop:flow,alert The action and scope that applied.     "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7",
    "dest_port": 443,
    "proto": "TCP",
    "tls": {
      "version": "TLS 1.3",
      "ja4": "t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb"
    },
    "alert": {
      "engine": "td",
      "action": "blocked",
      "signature_id": 900002,
      "signature": "Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"",
      "category": "A Network Trojan was detected",
      "severity": 1
    },
    "verdict": {
      "action": "drop"
    },
    "aws_metadata": {
      "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy"
    },
    "timestamp": "2026-11-11T06:15:26.671435+0000"
  }
}
Field Value What it tells you alert.engine td The IPS engine wrote this record. IPS records have no firewall object, because IPS rules don’t use hooks. tls.ja4 t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb The JA4 fingerprint of the client, which matches the fingerprint in the rule. alert.signature Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4) The IPS rule that matched, from the rule’s msg option. alert.category A Network Trojan was detected The rule’s classtype, trojan-activity, sets this category. verdict.action drop The IPS engine dropped the connection. aws_metadata.resource_arn arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy The rule is embedded in the policy, so the record shows the policy ARN. A match from an AWS managed rule group or one of your referenced rule groups carries that rule group’s ARN instead.

Validate in monitor mode, then enforce

Each Next Generation policy has a policy mode, enforce or monitor. In enforce mode, the engines apply their actions. In monitor mode, both engines evaluate your traffic and log what they would do. Your rules and the default action don’t drop or reject traffic.

  2. Send representative traffic for long enough to cover your normal patterns.
  3. In your alert logs, filter on engine = fw. Check the FirewallDefaultActionApplied metric in Amazon CloudWatch. Traffic that you meant to allow shouldn’t be reaching the default action.
  4. When the results look right, switch Policy mode to Enforce during a maintenance window. Changing the policy mode or the firewall default action restarts stateful inspection on the firewall, which interrupts established connections.

Figure 4 shows the policy and where each of the earlier log records comes from. items.title: Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.
items.summary: The short version An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password. Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys. We implemented containment measures, restored clean versions of the affected service, and have triggered a rotation of internal credentials. You do not need to update anything in your 1Password account. We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password, such as invitations or account recovery requests that you did not initiate. 1Password apps and services are working normally. What happened On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker. What information was affected The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include: Names and email addresses Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security) Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account) Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers) The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security. When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning . During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible. What was not affected Your vaults and the items in them The keys that protect your vaults 1Password does not store your account password or secret key Account recovery keys 1Password apps and browser extensions What we’ve done Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created. Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed. Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure. Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack. Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens. Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts. What happened

On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

What information was affected

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

  • Names and email addresses

  • Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

  • Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

  • Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

  • Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

  • Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.
